Able
ā'bl
a. (having power or capacity; rendering Hebrew yakol, Greek dunatos)
From the Latin habilis, apt, fit, from habeo, to have or hold. Hebrew yakol means to be able, to prevail, to endure; Greek dunatos is from dunamai, to be capable, and is the root of English dynamic.

Biblical Definition

Able is a small word that carries some of the largest confessions in Scripture, because it is the word faith uses about God when circumstances are against it. The three Hebrews standing before the furnace state it precisely: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king” (Daniel 3:17) — and their next words, but if not, show that ability confessed is not deliverance presumed. Paul uses the word for the reach of God's power beyond the limits of prayer and imagination: God is “able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). He uses it again in prison as the ground of his own settled confidence — “I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day” (2 Timothy 1:12) — where the object of trust is a Person, not a proposition. Jude closes with the same word turned toward perseverance: God is “able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy” (Jude 1:24). Taken together these say that the believer's security rests on divine ability, not human grip.

Webster 1828 Definition

Having sufficient power or capacity. In Scripture the characteristic word of faith about God — able to deliver, able to do above all we ask, able to keep from falling.

expand to see more

ABLE, a. [L. habilis, from habeo, to have or hold.] Having physical power sufficient; having competent power or strength, bodily or mental.

2. Having strong or unusual powers of mind; as, an able minister.

3. Having competent means or resources; as, able to bear the charge.

4. Having the requisite legal qualifications; as, able to inherit.

5. In Scripture, applied chiefly to God; as, God is able to make all grace abound, 2 Cor. 9.

Key Scripture

Daniel 3:17 — "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king."

Ephesians 3:20 — "Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,"

2 Timothy 1:12 — "For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day."

Jude 1:24 — "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,"

Modern Corruption

Able is now heard mainly in the vocabulary of human capacity and its measurement. Scripture's dominant use is the opposite — a confession of God's power made precisely where human capacity has run out.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's ordinary sense is stable; what has thinned is the habit of using it about God. Where an older piety said he is able, a functionally deist Christianity says we will do what we can, and prayer contracts to the size of what is already plausible. Ephesians 3:20 was written against exactly that contraction: God is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, so the ceiling is neither our request nor our imagination.

The principle to recover is the balance Daniel 3 strikes and modern usage loses in both directions. The three Hebrews neither doubted the ability nor presumed the outcome: our God is able to deliver, and he will deliver us out of thine hand — but if not, we still will not serve thy gods. Confessing God's ability is not a technique for securing a result, which is where prosperity teaching goes wrong, and declining to presume the result is not unbelief, which is where its critics sometimes overcorrect. Faith says able and then leaves the outcome with the one who is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yakol is to be able, to prevail, to endure. Greek dunamai is to be capable and dunatos the adjective; the compound hikanos adds the sense of sufficiency, being enough for the thing required.

expand to see more

Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail; used of God's power and of man's limits.

Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the verb behind the confession God is able.

Greek dunatos (G1415) — able, powerful; the adjective used of God in Romans 4:21.

Greek hikanos (G2425) — sufficient, competent, enough; Paul's word for ministerial sufficiency in 2 Corinthians 3:5.

Greek phulasso (G5442) — to guard, to keep; the verb Jude joins to able in able to keep you from falling.

Usage

"Of faith confessing power without presuming outcome: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us (Daniel 3:17)."

"Of God's reach beyond prayer and imagination: able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20)."

"Of the ground of perseverance: able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless (Jude 1:24)."
